report.source_text: Direct laryngoscopy revealed a submucosal cystic lesion immediately beneath the mobile vocal cords without any significant patent airway around the cyst (figure 2A). Using a 22-gauge microlaryngeal needle, 1 mL of thick yellowish clear fluid was aspirated from the cyst. The cyst arising from the right posterolateral wall of subglottis was marsupialised using coblator. Through the adequately patent airway tracheoscopy was performed which was unremarkable (figure 2B).

clinician.trajectory_summary: An 18-month-old girl presented with chronic and worsening respiratory distress, including noisy breathing, increased effort, and biphasic stridor, with a history of recurrent croup-like episodes and neonatal intubation. Physical examination confirmed signs of respiratory distress. Initial imaging (lateral neck radiograph and CT scan) revealed significant subglottic airway compromise and a hypodense, non-enhancing lesion in the subglottis, leading to a presumptive diagnosis of subglottic cyst. Following a negative COVID-19 test, the child underwent tracheotomy and direct laryngoscopy. Laryngoscopy confirmed a submucosal cystic lesion immediately beneath the mobile vocal cords, which was aspirated and marsupialized, resulting in an adequately patent airway.

Physical examination revealed irritability, tachypnoea, tachycardia without cyanosis, biphasic stridor with suprasternal and intercostal retraction worsening on crying and not relieved by postural changes.
Lateral neck radiograph showed significant subglottic airway compromise.
Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck revealed a hypodense, non-enhancing lesion measuring 9x8 mm in the subglottis.
A presumptive diagnosis of subglottic cyst was made, and a negative COVID-19 test was obtained prior to surgery.
Tracheotomy was performed, and direct laryngoscopy revealed a submucosal cystic lesion immediately beneath the mobile vocal cords without any significant patent airway around the cyst.
The subglottic cyst was aspirated (1 mL of thick yellowish clear fluid) and marsupialised using a coblator, resulting in an adequately patent airway.
